tldr: Weave is a unified framework that reconstructs reference motions from human interaction data while accounting for contact and grasp forces. It learns locomotion, whole-body balance, and multi-finger object manipulation within a single reinforcement learning policy. The policy achieves a 92.5% task success rate across nine everyday objects and demonstrates a 65.0% zero-shot success rate on interaction sequences unseen during training.
hero_caption: A single policy learned with Weave executes whole-body loco-manipulation in parallel across a diverse variety of everyday objects, including chairs, boxes, and coat racks. The entire sequence—approaching the object, establishing stable multi-finger grasps, lifting, and carrying—is coordinated seamlessly within one unified policy.
overview:
For humanoid robots to be useful in human environments, they must master whole-body loco-manipulation: walking up to an object, grasping it dexterously, and carrying it without losing balance. However, this is exceptionally challenging. It requires a single policy to simultaneously coordinate dynamic lower-body locomotion and millimeter-level fingertip contact control—two regimes operating at vastly different temporal and force scales.

Learning from human capture data is a promising approach, but human and robot anatomies differ. Simply copying joint angles often leaves fingertips falling short of surfaces or slipping off, failing to exert sufficient force. In addition, prior contact-rich manipulation studies typically train separate, dedicated policies for each object and motion, which severely limits generality.

To tackle this, the authors introduce Weave, a unified framework that explicitly and consistently handles contact information and 3D object geometry. It refines hand contacts from human demonstrations to satisfy force closure (grasps capable of resisting external disturbances) and uses a diffusion model to automatically complete approach locomotion toward the object, constructing physically executable robot reference trajectories. It then trains a single reinforcement learning policy conditioned on 3D object geometry and contact labels.

In extensive simulation experiments using the Unitree G1 robot (29-DoF body + 12-DoF hands), the single policy trained on nearly 8,000 trajectories across nine objects achieved a 92.5% success rate. Furthermore, the unified policy trained on all objects outperformed specialist models trained individually on single objects, highlighting a powerful synergy from multi-task learning.
contributions: Developed a unified policy that jointly controls whole-body locomotion, balance, multi-finger grasping, and carrying within a single model by explicitly accounting for contact information and 3D geometry.
Designed a pipeline that automatically constructs physically executable reference trajectories from human capture data through force-closure-aware grasp refinement and approach-motion completion.

Demonstrated that multi-object learning across nine objects outperforms single-object specialist models, and publicly released roughly 23 hours (~9,000 rollouts) of high-quality, physically executed rollout data.

sections.heading: Walk, Grasp, and Carry: Why Is Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation So Difficult?
sections.summary: Even everyday tasks like moving a chair tightly couple lower-body balance with delicate fingertip contact forces, making single-policy control extremely challenging. This paper presents Weave, which generates reference trajectories preserving geometry and contact relationships from human data to achieve coordinated whole-body control within a single policy.
sections.details:
When operating humanoid robots in environments designed for humans, walking up to an object, grasping it, and carrying it is one of the most fundamental and vital skills. Even moving a simple chair requires the robot to secure a multi-finger grasp and continuously adapt its whole-body posture in real time to counter the load. A tiny fingertip slip immediately shifts the upper-body load, and if lower-body balance fails, the robot topples along with the object. These elements form a deeply coupled problem.

Imitating human motion capture through reinforcement learning has gained significant traction. However, prior efforts have largely focused on coarse tracking of arm and torso trajectories while neglecting fingertip-level contact. Conversely, studies targeting dexterous hand manipulation typically isolate the hands on fixed bases or within CG character animations, bypassing walking dynamics. Because human and robot morphologies differ, simply copying joint angles fails to sustain the forces and torques needed to lift an object.

Another major barrier is whether a single policy can handle diverse objects and behaviors. Changing an object's geometry shifts valid grasp points, and altering the approach angle changes how the entire body must coordinate. Prior research often circumvented this by training individual policies per object, an approach that falls short of true general-purpose humanoid intelligence.

To overcome these hurdles, this work takes an approach that explicitly preserves 3D object geometry and hand-object contact throughout the entire pipeline. By retargeting motions to bridge morphological gaps while maintaining crucial contacts, the authors built Weave, a framework that trains a single policy across multiple objects and diverse interaction sequences.

sections.heading: From Motion Retargeting to Humanoid VLAs: Where Weave Stands
sections.summary: This section surveys three related research areas: contact-preserving motion retargeting, whole-body loco-manipulation, and large-scale VLA models. Weave faithfully reproduces fingertip-level physical contact while providing a reusable low-level skill foundation for future VLAs.
sections.details:
### II-A Contact-Preserving Retargeting and Motion Generation
When transferring human motions to robots, classical approaches optimized purely for joint position proximity. In object manipulation, however, floating just a few millimeters away from a surface breaks the interaction entirely. Consequently, recent methods incorporate contact topology and contact force consistency as explicit constraints. Meanwhile, advances in generative motion models like Kimodo make it possible to naturally synthesize missing approach locomotion. Weave combines these two paradigms to produce high-quality reference motions that can be tracked in physical simulation.

### II-B Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
Hierarchical architectures that decouple walking, approaching, grasping, and carrying are modular, but they struggle to manage contact forces and balance transitions across module boundaries. Conversely, end-to-end reinforcement learning methods excel at whole-body coordination, yet few venture into delicate multi-finger contact, and most still train dedicated policies per object. Weave departs from this by unifying fingertip-level contact and locomotion across multiple objects into a single tracking policy.

### II-C Relation to Humanoid Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Models
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that map language and vision directly to robot actions have generated immense excitement, but high-quality datasets coupling dynamic locomotion with high-DoF multi-finger manipulation remain scarce. The authors emphasize that Weave does not compete with VLAs; rather, it complements them. Weave provides physically grounded, robust low-level execution skills alongside high-quality rollout data, allowing future VLA models to focus on high-level task planning and skill selection.

sections.heading: Problem Formulation: Solving Whole-Body Coordination as a POMDP
sections.summary: The challenge of having a humanoid walk up to an object, grasp it, and carry it to a target is formulated as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). Synchronized robot-object reference trajectories built from human-object interactions serve as guides.
sections.details:
This work tackles the closed-loop control problem of a dexterous humanoid approaching an object, establishing a stable grasp, and transporting the object to a destination while sustaining whole-body balance. This is framed as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process $\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{O},\mathcal{T},r,\gamma)$.

At each timestep $t$, the policy consumes observation $o_t$ and outputs target joint position commands $a_t$ for low-level PD controllers. The action space $\mathcal{A}$ encompasses all whole-body joints across the torso, legs, and arms, as well as actuated finger joints in the multi-finger hands.

To facilitate sample-efficient reinforcement learning from scratch, the system builds upon captured human-object interaction (HOI) datasets. Processed through the proposed pipeline, these interactions become synchronized reference trajectories $\tau^{\mathrm{ref}}$ pairing robot poses $\hat{x}^{\mathrm{robot}}_t$ with object poses $\hat{x}^{\mathrm{obj}}_t$. These references serve both for Reference State Initialization during training and for computing tracking rewards.

sections.heading: Weave Architecture: From Reference Generation to Contact-Centric Policy Learning
sections.summary: Reference trajectories are built by retargeting human demonstrations to preserve contact and grasp forces, then synthesizing approach locomotion. Guided by these trajectories, the policy is trained via reinforcement learning using the modern Muon optimizer and a SimBaV2 backbone, with rewards shaped by 3D object geometry (SDF) and contact labels.
sections.details:
### IV-A Pipeline Overview
Weave consists of two primary stages. Stage 1 converts raw human motion capture data into physically plausible reference trajectories. Stage 2 trains a single policy using reinforcement learning (PPO) in simulation to jointly control all body and finger joints from these references.

### IV-B Building Contact-Preserving Reference Trajectories
To reconcile kinematic differences between humans and robots, the pipeline first solves whole-body inverse kinematics (IK). To prevent unrealistic vertical stretching, the pelvis is constrained only in the horizontal plane, optimizing its height based on ground contact.

However, standard IK only aligns gross arm poses, leaving fingertips misaligned with object surfaces. The pipeline resolves this with contact-aware hand refinement, adjusting only the arm and hand joints $\xi_t=(q_t^{\mathrm{arm}},q_t^{\mathrm{hand}})$. Specifically, it combines an objective pulling fingertips toward the object surface with an explicit, differentiable formulation of force closure quality $\hat{Q}_{\mathrm{FC}}$, which measures resistance to arbitrary external forces and torques. This yields hand poses that firmly pinch and grasp rather than merely touch.

Because raw capture clips typically begin right in front of the object, the Kimodo motion generation model completes the missing approach locomotion from initial positions. By sampling varied approach angles, the pipeline automatically expands single interaction clips into diverse approach paths. Finally, contact labels $\hat{c}_{t,\ell} \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ (separated, intermediate, in contact) are assigned to hand and foot links based on proximity to the object.

### IV-C Acquiring Contact Skills Through Reference Tracking
Reinforcement learning in simulation uses an asymmetric Actor-Critic setup. The Actor observes robot proprioception (joint positions, velocities), relative object pose, fingertip-to-surface vectors, contact flags, BPS-SDF features representing object geometry, and short-horizon future reference commands. The Critic additionally accesses privileged states, such as base translational velocity.

The reward function pairs pose tracking of the robot and object with a hand-opposition reward that encourages the thumb and fingers to pinch the object, alongside a contact-matching reward that checks alignment between reference contact labels and normalized contact forces. This prevents degenerate behaviors where the robot mimics the overall posture while keeping its hands open.

The policy architecture employs a SimBaV2 backbone featuring spherical normalization, paired with the Muon optimizer (orthogonalized momentum updates) for weight matrices and AdamW for biases and scaling terms.

captions.F2: The overall Weave pipeline. (a) Human capture demonstrations undergo (b) whole-body IK and force-closure-aware hand refinement, followed by (c) Kimodo-based approach-motion completion to generate complete reference trajectories. (d) Guided by these trajectories, a single policy powered by a SimBaV2 backbone learns diverse object manipulation skills in simulation.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Surprising Generalization in a Unified Policy
sections.summary: Experiments conducted on the Unitree G1 robot demonstrated a 92.5% success rate across nine trained objects and a 65.0% zero-shot success rate on unseen trajectories. Intriguingly, the single unified policy trained on all objects outperformed specialist models trained individually on single objects.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup
The platform comprises a Unitree G1 humanoid (29 body DoFs) equipped with Inspire dexterous hands (12 actuated DoFs across both hands). The dataset is split into training trajectories $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}$ (7,869 sequences, 19.56 hours) and test trajectories $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}$ (1,605 sequences, 3.67 hours) spanning nine objects, including chairs, tables, boxes, and coat racks. Metrics include Success Rate (SR), Progress Rate (PR), and tracking errors across links.

### V-B Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation Execution
Performance improved steadily throughout training. By 100k iterations, the policy reached a 92.5% success rate (96.3% progress rate) on the training set, with object position and orientation errors bounded to 4.27 cm and 7.18 degrees. This confirms that one policy can absorb roughly 8,000 diverse interaction trajectories without degradation.

Furthermore, when tested on unseen approach paths and motion sequences ($\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}$) without additional training, it achieved a 65.0% success rate (84.5% progress rate). Although the test set deliberately introduces wider approach angles that cause distributional shift, the policy maintained robust adaptability.

### V-C Single Unified Model vs. Object Specialists
A particularly notable comparison evaluated the unified policy trained on all nine objects against nine separate specialist models trained individually on single objects. When matched for computational resources (total training iterations), the pooled success rate of the unified policy reached 95.3%, outperforming the specialists' 91.5%. The unified policy surpassed specialists on six objects and matched them on the remaining three, showing no regression on any object.

A key takeaway is that lower tracking error does not equate to higher task success. Specialists overfit to single-object trajectories, lowering imitation error at the expense of recovery margins against disturbances. In contrast, by handling diverse objects simultaneously, the unified policy discovers shared coordination primitives—such as steady walking posture and shared grasp topologies between small and large tables—yielding a more robust, fall-resistant controller.

### V-D Architectural and Optimizer Contributions
Ablations comparing network architectures (SimBaV2 vs. standard MLP) and optimizers (Muon vs. AdamW) revealed that Muon drove early sample efficiency gains. Because the reward landscape blends coarse whole-body tracking with sensitive fingertip contact, gradient scales differ dramatically. Under AdamW, large whole-body gradients dominate, causing the policy to settle into local minima where it matches poses with open hands. Muon's orthogonalized momentum updates equalize updates across these scales, while SimBaV2's spherical normalization dampens policy volatility, enabling rapid and stable convergence.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Limitations: Steps Toward Real-World Deployment
sections.summary: Weave establishes a robust framework for learning whole-body dexterous loco-manipulation from human demonstrations and contributes ~23 hours of high-quality rollout data. The authors also outline current limitations, including simulation-only privileged state reliance, underactuated hands, and the need for high-level planner integration.
sections.details:
Weave successfully translates captured human object interactions into high-fidelity whole-body skills executable by humanoid robots. By explicitly modeling contact and geometry, a single policy orchestrates walking, balance, multi-finger grasping, and transport, producing a physically consistent rollout dataset spanning roughly 23 hours (~9,000 trajectories).

Nonetheless, the authors identify several key limitations:
First, all experiments were conducted in simulation relying on ground-truth state estimates. Transferring to real hardware will require on-board state estimation, distillation into vision-based policies, and closing the contact-rich Sim2Real gap.
Second, the Inspire hands are underactuated (controlling only proximal joints while distal joints couple mechanically), precluding intricate in-hand dexterous manipulation. Very heavy objects and articulated multi-body objects also remain out of scope.
Third, the policy operates strictly as a reference-tracking controller. Enabling autonomous decisions about what to move and where to carry it will require integrating Weave's execution skills with high-level humanoid VLA models and task planners.

takeaways: Imitating contact-rich motions requires refining hand poses to satisfy force closure (resisting external forces) rather than relying solely on kinematic joint matching.

Training across multiple objects within a single policy reinforces shared patterns of whole-body balance and grasp geometry, outperforming dedicated single-object specialist models in both success rate and generalization.

In reinforcement learning problems with stark gradient disparities—such as coarse locomotion coupled with delicate fingertip contact—pairing an orthogonalized momentum optimizer like Muon with normalized architectures like SimBaV2 effectively averts degenerate local optima.
Low tracking error does not guarantee task success; robust whole-body contact control demands prioritizing disturbance recovery margins over rigid reference imitation.
limitations: Experiments are limited to simulation with ground-truth odometry and object poses; real-world Sim2Real transfer remains unverified.
The robot hands are underactuated (proximal joints only) and tested objects are limited to rigid bodies, excluding fine in-hand manipulation and articulated objects.
The policy strictly tracks provided reference trajectories and lacks integration with high-level planners or VLAs capable of autonomous, context-driven task reasoning.
